## Ezekiel 16:22–42 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 22 — "And in all your abominations and acts of prostitution, you did not remember the days of your youth when you were naked and bare, wallowing in your own blood."

- **Gill:** The "abominations and whoredoms" are idolatries, which were many and abominable to God. The failure to "remember" means Israel forgot their miserable, destitute condition in Egypt and all that God had done for them — a deep ingratitude. Their forgetting what God had delivered them from removed any check on their idolatries. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/16-22.html)

- **Calvin:** God here proves the people's extreme wickedness: if they had remembered the wretched slavery from which they were delivered, they would not have been so blinded by pride. Forgetting God's benefits led to lascivious self-confidence and foul idolatries. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/16-22.html)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The words gain fuller significance when compared with Jeremiah 2:2 — the Husband (God) remembered "the love of her espousals," but the faithless wife forgot the life of shame and misery from which she had been rescued. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/16-22.html)

- **Matthew Henry:** Forgetting their beginning is listed as one of the three root causes of Israel's sin (alongside pride and weakness of heart). "It should be an effectual check to our pride and sensuality to consider what we are and how much we are beholden to the free grace of God." (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC26016.HTM)

- **Enduring Word (David Guzik):** Israel's haughty pride was rooted in their failure to remember their poor and humble beginning, and how all protection, provision, and adornment were God's gift. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Trapp:** "Hence all thy haughtiness and hauntiness. We should often say, as that noble Iphicrates the Athenian once did, 'From how small to how great matters hath the Lord raised me!'" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 23 — "Woe! Woe to you, declares the Lord GOD. And in addition to all your other wickedness…"

- **Enduring Word:** The repeated "Woe, woe" is God's sorrowful lament over wicked Israel, coming from great depth of feeling. Feinberg adds that "the repeated woe is partly threat and partly lament." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Matthew Henry:** This "woe" introduces the fact that after all previous wickedness (idolatry, child sacrifice), Jerusalem added yet more — building shrines and high places everywhere. (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC26016.HTM)

---

### v. 24 — "You built yourself a mound and made yourself a lofty shrine in every public square."

- **Enduring Word:** As Israel worsened, idolatry multiplied and spread everywhere. Clarke notes that the Hebrew word translated "shrine" (*gab*) can mean "a stew or brothel" — Coverdale's Bible (1535) rendered it: "Thou hast builded thy stewes and bordell houses in every place." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Matthew Henry:** They "adorned their idol-temples, and groves, and high places" — multiplying places of false worship throughout the land aggressively. (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC26016.HTM)

---

### v. 25 — "At the head of every street you built your lofty shrines and degraded your beauty. With increasing promiscuity, you spread your legs to all who passed by."

- **Enduring Word:** The phrase "you offered yourself" (NKJV) is literally "you opened your feet" — Ezekiel used deliberately shocking language to jolt his jaded listeners. Israel's unfaithfulness was not only everywhere in place, but to every passing god. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Trapp:** "And hast made thy beauty to be abhorred — by being made so cheap and common. Sin is a reproach to any people, idolatry especially." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 26 — "You prostituted yourself with your lustful neighbors, the Egyptians, and increased your promiscuity to provoke Me to anger."

- **Enduring Word:** Israel's unfaithfulness extended even to the gods of the Egyptians, described as "very fleshly neighbors" (NKJV) — a reference to the sexually-charged nature of Egyptian idolatry. They did all this deliberately to provoke God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Matthew Henry:** They "worshipped all the idols that came in their way… ready to close with every temptation of this kind, though ever so absurd. No foreign idol could be imported, no new god invented, but they were ready to catch at it, as a common strumpet that prostitutes herself to all comers." (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC26016.HTM)

---

### v. 27 — "Therefore I stretched out My hand against you and reduced your portion. I gave you over to the desire of those who hate you, the daughters of the Philistines, who were ashamed of your lewd conduct."

- **Ellicott:** "Diminished thine ordinary food — This cutting short of the power and prosperity of Israel was a discipline of correction designed to bring her to a consciousness of her sin." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Whedon:** "Her fixed or allotted support was lessened, just as an insulted husband would take something from the wife's stipend." The reference seems to be to "the distant times of Philistine supremacy in the last days of the judges." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/ezekiel-16.html)

- **StudyLight (general):** The Philistines — themselves pagan — were "ashamed of thy lewd way," meaning Israel's conduct was so degraded that even the pagan Philistines found it scandalous. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/16-22.html)

- **Matthew Henry:** "God rebuked them, but still they continued in the same sins." The diminishing of their portion was a corrective judgment, but Israel did not respond with repentance. (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC26016.HTM)

---

### v. 28 — "Then you prostituted yourself with the Assyrians, because you were not yet satisfied. Even after that, you were still not satisfied."

- **StudyLight (Henderson via Lange):** "Not satisfied with adopting the idolatories of Egypt, the Jews practised those of the more distant Assyrians and Babylonians. They were perfectly insatiable in their lust. Their idolatry was an amalgamation of all the different forms which obtained in the countries around them." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/16-22.html)

- **Whedon:** Not content with Canaanitish and Egyptian idolatry (vv. 20, 26), she turned "for novelties of wickedness to the Assyrians and Chaldeans." The phrase "thou hast provoked me in all these ways, adding one sin upon another, because thy whoredoms were too few for thee" (quoting Mosheh Ben Shesheth). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 29 — "So you extended your promiscuity to Chaldea, the land of merchants — but even with this you were not satisfied!"

- **Whedon:** "Unto the merchants' land, even unto Chaldea" (compare Ezekiel 17:4). Israel pursued alliances and idolatries all the way to Babylon — yet nothing satisfied. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/ezekiel-16.html)

- **StudyLight (Henderson):** The insatiable pursuit of new lovers (foreign alliances and their gods) demonstrated a diseased craving: their idolatry was an amalgamation of every form practiced by surrounding nations. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/16-22.html)

---

### v. 30 — "How weak-willed is your heart, declares the Lord GOD, while you do all these things, the acts of a shameless prostitute!"

- **StudyLight (Henderson):** Some render this "Yet how languishing is thine heart" — a sickly craving of lustful desire grown into a disease. Others understand it of sin's general tendency to weaken moral nature: "The influence of sin on the soul is to render it morally impotent… the individual allows [habits] to grow upon him, so that he becomes at last insensible to the operation of the strongest moral motives." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/16-22.html)

- **Matthew Henry:** "The strength of men's lusts is an evidence of the weakness of their hearts; they have no acquaintance with themselves, nor government of themselves. She is weak, and yet an imperious whorish woman. Those that are most foolish are commonly most imperious, and think themselves fit to manage others when they are far from being able to manage themselves." (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC26016.HTM)

---

### vv. 31–34 — Worse Than a Prostitute: She Pays Instead of Being Paid

- **Enduring Word:** Israel becomes worse than a literal prostitute: a prostitute at least receives payment, but Israel scorned payment, gave herself away for free, and even bribed her lovers. This shows the sheer irrationality and hardness of heart behind her unfaithfulness. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Whedon on v. 31:** "In scoffing at [her] hire" — the ordinary prostitute scoffs at the first sum and waits for a larger inducement, "but this insatiable woman actually pays hire instead of receiving it (see 2 Kings 16:8). The meaning is that she prizes foreign alliances and religions far more than these foreigners prize hers." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/ezekiel-16.html)

- **StudyLight (Henderson):** Israel gave presents to its lovers, contrary to the practice of prostitutes in general. The Jews practiced idolatry not from the mere love of gain, but from the gratification they found in that sin. "They had arrived at that lowest stage of depravity when sin is loved merely for its own sake." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/16-22.html)

- **Matthew Henry (v. 32):** She is worse than a common harlot — she is "as a wife that committeth adultery, which taketh strangers instead of her husband." This is the core of the sin: covenant-breaking. The wife already has a husband providing for her, yet she seeks strangers, making the betrayal far worse. (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC26016.HTM)

---

### v. 35 — "Therefore, O prostitute, hear the word of the LORD!"

- **Preacher's Complete Homiletical (Lange/Keil):** At this point the address turns from accusation to the announcement of punishment. The direct summons "O harlot, hear the word of the LORD" marks the transition from indictment to sentencing. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Ellicott:** The prophet, having described the sin, now turns to pronounce the punishment. The same allegory is preserved throughout. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 36 — "Because you poured out your wealth and exposed your nakedness in your promiscuity with your lovers and with all your detestable idols, and because of the blood of your children which you gave to them…"

- **Preacher's Complete Homiletical (Hengstenberg):** The Hebrew literally reads "Because thy brass has been lavished" — "brass" (copper money) signifies money generally. Israel had spent the wealth God gave her in the service of idolatry. The "paramours" are the world-powers themselves, and with them the heathen gods whose worship followed political dependence. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** "Thy filthiness" is literally "thy brass" — either alluding to tribute money (v. 34) or a symbol of shame and vileness (like our "brazen faced"). "By the blood of thy children" may refer especially to the Molech sacrifices of v. 21, but also includes the lavish waste of life and treasure from foreign alliances. The harlot city is also a murderess. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/16-22.html)

---

### v. 37 — "Therefore I will surely gather all the lovers with whom you found pleasure, all those you loved and all those you hated. I will gather them against you from all around and expose you before them, and they will see you completely naked."

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The "lovers" are the nations with which Judah had allied herself and whose religion she adopted — Moabites, Ammonites, Syrians, Philistines, Edomites, and Chaldeans. Both those she loved and those she hated would exult in her shame and fall (cf. Psalm 137:7; 2 Kings 24:2). (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/16-37.html)

- **Preacher's Complete Homiletical (Lange):** "The public judgment. First of all, the assembling of the lovers as witnesses. She who has dishonoured and brought herself to shame becomes now, by the interposition of God, to the one party an object of loathing, to the other an object of mockery. The last attraction, and what might still have been an object of regard, vanishes." Hävernick refers to the procedure for a married woman suspected of adultery (Numbers 5:18). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Whedon:** "Her judges shall be her lovers, whom she, like Ishtar, has welcomed and discarded one by one." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 38 — "And I will sentence you to the punishment of women who commit adultery and those who shed blood; so I will bring upon you the wrath of your bloodshed and jealousy."

- **Preacher's Complete Homiletical (Keil):** This explains the figurative language of v. 37. Israel was to be punished with the punishment of adulterers and murderers. "Thou shalt be turned into blood, so that nothing but blood may be left of thee, and that the blood of fury and jealousy, as the working of the wrath and jealousy of God." The heathen will destroy all objects of idolatry, then take clothes and jewellery, leave her naked, and execute death by stoning and by sword — destroying both city and kingdom. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** Strictly, the punishment of the adulteress was death by stoning (Leviticus 20:2, 10; Deuteronomy 21:21; 22:21; John 8:5). Ezekiel may have thought of the stones cast against Jerusalem from Chaldean catapult engines as a literal counterpart. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 39 — "Then I will deliver you into the hands of your lovers, and they will level your mounds and tear down your lofty shrines. They will strip off your clothes, take your fine jewelry, and leave you naked and bare."

- **Preacher's Complete Homiletical (Hengstenberg):** "As thou wast before the Lord had mercy on thee (Ezekiel 16:7). The unfaithful use of the gifts of God inevitably brings on their loss. God cannot be mocked." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Preacher's Complete Homiletical (homiletical notes):** "When we abuse the mercies of God, we give Him cause to take them away… God would give them into their hands who should rob them of their fair jewels, and strip them of all their clothes… He found her naked, and now He would leave her naked and bare. When God hath showed much kindness to a people, and they have been ungrateful, He will reduce them to their former condition." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 40 — "They will bring a mob against you, who will stone you and cut you to pieces with their swords."

- **Preacher's Complete Homiletical (Keil):** "This may be explained from the ancient mode of administering justice, according to which the popular assembly (Proverbs 5:14) sat in judgment on cases of adultery and capital crimes, and executed the sentence, as the law for stoning expressly enjoins (Leviticus 20:2; Numbers 15:36; Deuteronomy 22:21). But they are also applicable to the foes, who would march against Jerusalem." Stoning was the usual mode of capital punishment under Mosaic law for idolatry, adultery, and murder. This doom was accomplished literally, for Jerusalem was "stoned" before she was burned (Jeremiah 33:4). Slaying with the sword was the doom for those who seduced men to apostasy (Deuteronomy 13:12–15). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Enduring Word:** The "assembly" against Jerusalem refers to the gathering of enemy armies (the Babylonians) who would execute God's judgment. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

---

### v. 41 — "Then they will burn down your houses and execute judgment against you in the sight of many women. I will put an end to your prostitution, and you will never again pay your lovers."

- **Preacher's Complete Homiletical (Keil/Klieforth):** "The many women are the many heathen nations, according to the description of Jerusalem or Israel as an unfaithful wife." Klieforth adds: "As it is the greatest punishment to an adulterous woman to be exposed in her sin before the eyes of other women; so will the severest portion of Israel's punishment be, that it will stand exposed in its sin before the eyes of all other nations." The burning of houses was fulfilled in 2 Kings 25:8–9. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Ellicott:** "Shall burn thine house — Comp. Deuteronomy 13:16. The figurative and the literal sense here blend together; the house of the unfaithful wife shall be destroyed, and the houses of Jerusalem shall be burned." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Preacher's Complete Homiletical (Hengstenberg):** "And thou also shalt give no hire any more — Because thou wilt have no more lovers; wilt, on the whole, after the dissolution of thy national independence, be no more in a condition which admits of impure intercourse with the world-powers." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Gill:** After the Babylonian captivity, the Jews never returned to idolatry any more — the punishment accomplished its purpose of ending that specific sin. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/16-42.html)

---

### v. 42 — "So I will lay to rest My wrath against you, and My jealousy will turn away from you. Then I will be calm and no longer angry."

- **Gill (two interpretations):** (1) When the Jews ceased their idolatries after the Babylonian captivity, God's fury and its effects ceased — God no longer contends with a people than while they are sinning. (2) Alternatively, some render it "I will make my fury to rest upon thee" — wrath abiding until an utter end. However, Gill prefers the first sense because it agrees with what precedes and follows. The jealousy departs as when a man has utterly rejected his adulterous wife, or when a wife returns and lives chastely. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/16-42.html)

- **Clarke:** "I will be quiet and will be no more angry. — I will completely abandon thee; have nothing more to do with thee; think no more of thee. When God in judgment ceases to reprehend, this is the severest judgment." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Ellicott:** "My fury… to rest — Not in pity but in satiety, as having accomplished the utter desolation of Israel." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Preacher's Complete Homiletical (Hengstenberg):** "The jealousy ceases because it has found its satisfaction in their punishment, and exhausted itself therein, as the fire ceases when it has consumed its fuel." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Preacher's Complete Homiletical (Lange):** "The Divine justice comes to an end in its character of jealousy — in other words, as the injured faithfulness and love of Israel's husband. The departing of the jealousy might, perhaps, by comparison with Isaiah 11:13, show grace in the background; but the connection with what follows requires rather a thought like Hosea 2:4. Jehovah gives up the adulterous whorish wife." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The words are not primarily of comfort but of the satisfaction of the jealous husband's righteous anger — a completed punishment. Yet that thought was "the beginning of hope for the future," as the sequel shows (vv. 53, 60–63). "The injured husband, in the bold anthropomorphic language of the parable, would be no more angry. The Lord God of Israel would remember his covenant, and forgive." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Whedon:** "Make my fury toward thee to rest — Literally, satisfy my fury upon thee. (See Ezekiel 16:13.)" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/ezekiel-16.html)

---

## Protestant Traditions: Areas of Difference

### The Meaning of God's Wrath "Resting" (v. 42)

This is where the most notable divergence emerges:

- **Baptist (Gill, Calvinistic Baptist, 1746):** Emphasizes that God's fury ceases because the sin ceases — after the Babylonian exile, Israel abandoned idolatry. God's jealousy departs either because He has divorced the unfaithful wife or because she returns and lives chastely. There is a note of possible restoration. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/16-42.html)

- **Reformed/Calvinist (Calvin, Ellicott, Hengstenberg):** The emphasis is on the satisfying of divine justice through punishment. Ellicott says the fury rests "not in pity but in satiety." Hengstenberg says jealousy ceases "as the fire ceases when it has consumed its fuel." The wrath is exhausted in the destruction. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Methodist/Arminian leaning (Clarke):** Takes the most severe view — "I will completely abandon thee; have nothing more to do with thee… When God in judgment ceases to reprehend, this is the severest judgment." God's quietness is abandonment, not peace. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik/Enduring Word):** The closing of vv. 40–43 is presented within the larger arc of the chapter that ends with God remembering His covenant and promising an everlasting covenant (vv. 60–63), hinting at atonement. The judgment is real but not final — restoration follows. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Lutheran (Lange, cited in Preacher's Homiletical):** Sees the departing of jealousy as potentially showing "grace in the background" (by comparison with Isaiah 11:13), but notes the immediate context rather requires a thought like Hosea 2:4 — "Jehovah gives up the adulterous whorish wife." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-16.html)

### The Identity of "Many Women" (v. 41)

All major Protestant commentators agree these represent the surrounding heathen nations who witness Jerusalem's judgment. Keil says explicitly "the many women are the many heathen nations." Klieforth notes the shame-element: the greatest punishment to an adulteress is exposure before other women. No significant denominational difference was found on this point in the sources consulted.

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship

- **NET Bible notes:** Not directly available from the pages fetched. However, the scholarship cited by Enduring Word (Block, Taylor, Wright) represents modern critical scholarship mediating the text for evangelical readers. Block in particular notes that "cutting the cord, washing, rubbing down with salt, and clothing the newborn were also customary legal acts of legitimation" and that the abandonment of the infant legally relinquished all rights and responsibilities — cultural background that illuminates the metaphor. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings

- No specific Catholic or Orthodox commentary on these verses was found within the search results from the permitted Catholic/Orthodox sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org). The searches did not return relevant results from those domains for Ezekiel 16:22–42. This section remains unfilled from the available sources.
